extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor unions, labor-relations professionals, human-resources staff, and labor attorneys (stakeholders affected by or commenting on NLRB joint-employer rulemaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Final rule and regulatory preamble describing the National Labor Relations Board's standard for identifying joint employers under the NLRA, including definitions, elements, burdens, and related regulatory-impact analyses relevant to employers, unions, and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint employers — general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For all purposes under the Act, two or more employers of the same particular employees are joint employers of those employees if the employers share or codetermine those matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central definitional standard (§103.40(b)). It is grounded in common-law agency principles (see §103.40(a)) and is the threshold inquiry for applying the Act's obligations and protections to multiple entities that affect the same employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'share or codetermine' (authority to control)
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'share or codetermine those matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment' means for an employer to possess the authority to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), or to exercise the power to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), one or more of the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the operative concept of control for joint-employer status (§103.40(c)). The rule focuses on authority or the power to control, not merely on other indicia of commercial relationship. Possession of authority can be direct or indirect and may be sufficient even if not exercised (see also §103.40(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of 'essential terms and conditions of employment'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Essential terms and conditions of employment' are (1) wages, benefits, and other compensation; (2) hours of work and scheduling; (3) the assignment of duties to be performed; (4) the supervision of the performance of duties; (5) work rules and directions governing the manner, means, and methods of the performance of duties and the grounds for discipline; (6) the tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge; and (7) working conditions related to the safety and health of employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven categories (§103.40(d)(1)-(7)) are the concrete matters that the Board will evaluate to determine whether employers 'share or codetermine' essential terms and conditions. Evidence of authority over one or more of these matters can establish joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessing authority to control is sufficient (exercise not required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing the authority to control one or more essential terms and conditions of employment is sufficient to establish status as a joint employer, regardless of whether control is exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in §103.40(e)(1) and supported by cited precedent, this principle means that reserved contractual or legal authority to control (even if never used) can establish joint-employer status. The preamble cites longstanding case law endorsing the 'right to control' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercising indirect power to control suffices (including through an intermediary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercising the power to control indirectly (including through an intermediary) one or more essential terms and conditions of employment is sufficient to establish status as a joint employer, regardless of whether the power is exercised directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §103.40(e)(2) clarifies that indirect mechanisms of control (e.g., via contractors, supervisors provided through a staffing firm, or contractual arrangements) can create joint-employer status. The preamble explains the Board's approach to the 'indirect-control' element in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of control over immaterial matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of an entity's control over matters that are immaterial to the existence of an employment relationship under common-law agency principles and that do not bear on the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment is not relevant to the determination of whether the entity is a joint employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §103.40(f) prevents use of evidence about control over nonessential/commercial matters (e.g., purely contractual business objectives) from establishing joint-employer status. The focus must remain on control that bears on the essential terms and conditions listed in §103.40(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for asserting joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting that an employer is a joint employer of particular employees has the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the entity meets the requirements set forth in paragraphs (a) through (f) of this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §103.40(g) places the evidentiary burden on the party alleging joint-employer status and specifies the ordinary civil standard ('preponderance of the evidence'). This guides adjudicative fact-finding in Board proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining obligations of a joint employer
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer of particular employees (1) must bargain collectively with the representative of those employees with respect to any term and condition of employment that it possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control, regardless of whether that term or condition is deemed to be an essential term and condition of employment under this section for the purposes of establishing joint-employer status; but (2) is not required to bargain with respect to any term and condition of employment that it does not possess the authority to control or exercise the power to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §103.40(h)(1)-(2) explains the practical consequences of joint-employer status: entities must bargain over matters they have authority to control, even if those matters were not used to establish joint-employer status, and need not bargain over matters outside their control. This can affect remediation and collective-bargaining obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of the section's provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of this section are intended to be severable. If any paragraph of this section is held to be unlawful, the remaining paragraphs of this section not deemed unlawful are intended to remain in effect to the fullest extent permitted by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §103.40(i) signals that individual provisions are meant to stand independently to preserve as much of the rule as possible in the event a court invalidates part of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA requirement to assess reporting, recordkeeping, and compliance burdens on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires an agency to consider the direct burden that compliance with a new regulation will likely impose on small entities, including the amount of 'reporting, recordkeeping and other compliance requirements' imposed on small entities, and allows either quantifiable/numerical descriptions or 'more general descriptive statements if quantification is not practicable or reliable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble discussion (FRFA section) describes the Board's obligation to analyze small-entity impacts and to solicit comment. The Board concluded the final rule imposes no capital costs, no new information-collection requirements, and no direct costs of modifying processes, hiring for compliance, or lost sales/profits attributable to the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA indicators for 'significant economic impact' on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria to consider include: whether the rule will cause long-term insolvency; whether the cost of the proposed regulation will (a) eliminate more than 10 percent of the businesses' profits; (b) exceed one percent of the gross revenues of the entities in a particular sector; or (c) exceed five percent of the labor costs of the entities in the sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the specific economic benchmarks the Board uses to determine whether compliance costs are 'significant' within the meaning of the RFA. The Board applied these indicators in concluding the rule's familiarization costs are not significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating familiarization costs to small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board estimates that a human-resources or labor-relations specialist at a small employer may take at most one hour to read the text of the rule and supplementary information; a small employer may also consult an attorney for one hour. Using BLS wage and benefit costs, the Board estimated labor costs between $208.60 and $227.98 for small employers and $169.11 for unions to review and understand the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Board's applied method and numeric estimate for assessing the time-cost burden of understanding the rule. It is an example of how the Board quantified (or estimated) compliance familiarization costs for the FRFA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board explained that the proposed rule would not impose any information collection requirements and, accordingly, the proposed rule is not subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501-3521).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble PRA analysis: because there are no new information-collection burdens, the agency concluded PRA procedures do not apply. Agencies must still consider and respond to comments on PRA applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act procedural designation
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of this rule are substantive. Therefore, the Board will submit this rule and required accompanying information to the Senate, the House of Representatives, and the Comptroller General as required by the Congressional Review Act. OIRA will designate this rule as a 'major rule' if it will have an effect on the economy of more than $100 million during the year it takes effect, and the rule will become effective no earlier than 60 days after its publication in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies CRA filing and timing consequences (submission to Congress and GAO and potential 'major rule' designation), which affects the rule's effective date and congressional oversight.
